catalog_quote: 2.9 Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length, as in the common Wakka-Wakka greeting wanḑá ŋin janánde where (i.e. how) are you going? Here we have two stress units, of which the former consists of two words or morphological elements; similarly in Goreng-Goreng: gilámanmin turned round, Goeng-Goeng wajálara (mountain name), goréŋ goréŋ (language name), etc. This tendency also explains the origin of certain shortened forms, e.g. (Wakka-Wakka) ga not (< waga), ḑu I (< ŋaḑu), (Barunggam) ɲaŋgu why? (< *miɲaŋgu), ɲuŋga where? (< waɲuŋga), etc. Compare the common stress pattern in Aboriginal place names of the type 'Cutháraba', 'Didíllibah', 'Barálaba', all over Queensland.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Holmer says stress is not significant (not distinctive) in Goreng-Goreng or any language of the survey, but that there is a pervasive tendency to stress the second syllable of a word or of a longer stress unit (gilámanmin, goréŋ goréŋ; cf. place names Cutháraba, Barálaba). The reading 'fixed: second syllable' records that phonetic tendency; the source's own characterisation is 'stress not significant'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Goreng-Goreng. In the same survey Holmer remarks for Bidjara (Part II §8.5, p. 205) that beside the second-syllable accent 'secondary stress appear[s] on subsequent alternate syllables' (bibanagána), presented as the same general tendency ('As pointed out in Part I, 2.9'), but not stated for Goreng-Goreng.
new_statements.exceptions: Endnote 14 (p. 161): a Wakka-Wakka informant claim that bala· 'jewfish' and bala 'semen' differ 'with a different stress and vowel quantity' 'finds no support from further investigation'. Manandjali §9.6 (p. 413) restricts the tendency to words of at least three syllables, but the Goreng-Goreng example goréŋ goréŋ is disyllabic.
new_statements.domain_note: Blanket statement over all languages of the survey (Wakka group incl. Goreng-Goreng, Gunggari group, others), with one Goreng-Goreng word and the language name as examples. Domain is 'words or utterances of some length'; Holmer explicitly allows a stress unit to span two words (wanɖá ŋin), so the tendency is as much phrasal as lexical. Data from a single chief informant (Reggie Dodd, Goreng-Goreng mother, Wakka-Wakka father) whom Holmer himself says may have mixed the two languages (§13.1, p. 89).
new_statements.identity_note: Holmer 1983 calls the language 'Goreng-Goreng', the upper Burnett River language (Mount Perry, Eidsvold, Cracow area) = Glottolog gure1255 / AIATSIS E32 / ISO gnr; the same sentence gives a separate example for 'Goeng-Goeng' (AIATSIS E36; Glottolog treats Goeng-Goeng under gure1255's neighbour set, Holmer calls them closely related variants). Wikipedia files the language under 'Taribelang' (E33) and notes the E33/E36 confusion. Holmer's chief informant (Reggie Dodd) had a Wakka-Wakka father and Holmer warns (§13.1, p. 89) that early material may mix Wakka-Wakka; the stress remark is a survey-wide generalisation with one Goreng-Goreng example, not a language-specific analysis.

Goreng-Goreng chapter (pp. 89-104) phonology §14.1 (p. 90) says phonemes are those of Wakka-Wakka and refers back to the general sections; no separate stress remark. Endnote 14 (p. 161): a Wakka-Wakka claim of a stress/quantity contrast bala· vs bala not supported.
